title: Regulatable membrane-bound IL-15 engineered TIL cell therapy for immune checkpoint inhibitor-resistant advanced melanoma: pooled analysis of phase 1 and 1/2 trials
desc: Amsokigene autoleucel (amsoki-cel, OBX-115) is a tumor-infiltrating lymphocyte (TIL) cell therapy engineered to express acetazolamide (ACZ)-regulatable membrane-bound interleukin-15, abrogating the need for interleukin-2. In two single-arm trials (completed phase 1 single-center first-in-human (FIH) and ongoing phase 1/2 multicenter Agni-01), patients with immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI)-resistant advanced melanoma received lymphodepletion and varying doses and schedules of amsoki-cel and ACZ. The primary objective of FIH and Agni-01 phase 1 was safety, tolerability and recommended phase 2 dose (RP2D); the primary objective of Agni-01 phase 2 was objective response rate (ORR) at the RP2D. The first patient treated experienced rapid lymphocyte expansion and vasogenic edema of a previously irradiated brain metastasis, prompting protocol modifications and dose deescalation in FIH, including 80% reduction in maximum amsoki-cel dose and 75% reduction in ACZ dose. After preliminary demonstration of safety at the lower dose, doses were increased in FIH, and reescalation was initiated in Agni-01. Across studies, 37 patients were treated (FIH, n = 17; Agni-01, n = 20). Post hoc pooled analysis demonstrated no dose-limiting toxicities, ICU care or treatment-related mortality. Most common grade 3 or higher treatment-emergent adverse events (TEAEs) included neutropenia (64.9% (24/37)), leukopenia/lymphopenia (56.8% (21/37) each) and anemia/thrombocytopenia (37.8% (14/37) each). Serious TEAEs were reported for 10 patients, including eight patients with grade 3 or higher events (non-hematologic, 13.5% (5/37); hematologic, 13.5% (5/37)). RP2D was selected based on overall safety and tolerability as well as preliminary anti-tumor activity in Agni-01 phase 1. The phase 2 preliminary ORR was 66.7% (6/9). In total, 15 patients were treated at RP2D and comprise the Key Efficacy Set (Agni-01: phase 1, n = 6; phase 2, n = 9), of which 10 patients (66.7%; 95% confidence interval 38−88%) achieved objective responses (including two complete responses). Amsoki-cel demonstrated favorable safety and promising early clinical activity in patients with ICI-resistant melanoma. A separate phase 2 pivotal Agni-01 cohort is ongoing. ClinicalTrials.gov identifiers: NCT05470283 and NCT06060613 . title: Emerging applications of machine learning and AI for predictive modeling in precision medicine
desc: Pure data-driven artificial intelligence (AI) is insufficient for clinical adoption. This editorial summarizes 31 papers showing that precision medicine requires integrating structural domain knowledge before model training. We identify three necessary transitions: anchoring algorithms in biological laws for mechanistic interpretability; designing collaborative, human-centered clinical interfaces; and scaling equitable, population-level interventions. These shifts advance medical AI from technical novelty toward trustworthy, clinically grounded, and ethically deployed foundational science.

title: Efficacy and implementation of augmented reality in healthcare: a scoping review in randomized controlled trials.
source: PubMed · International journal of medical informatics
desc: [International journal of medical informatics] Despite medical advances, significant challenges in routine practice persist, including diagnostic variability from traditional two-dimensional (2D) imaging, surgical risks due to anatomical uncertainty, and poor patient comprehension that contributes to perioperative anxiety. Augmented Reality (AR) offers a solution by overlaying three-dimensional (3D) digital information onto the real-world environment, providing real-time guidance to address these clinical gaps. However, while AR's clinical efficacy is increasingly proven, its practical integration into standard clinical workflows remains fragmented. This study presents a scoping review restricted to RCT-level evidence to systematically map the scope, distinct clinical capabilities, implementation limitations, and ethical frameworks of AR-based healthcare systems. A systematic search was conducted across PubMed and Embase to identify randomized controlled trials involving AR interventions in healthcare. Methodological quality was appraised using the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) Critical Appraisal Checklist. A total of 25 Randomized Controlled Trials (RCTs) were analyzed and categorized based on clinical domains (education, diagnosis, intervention, and rehabilitation) and their functional roles (delivering or assisting). AR was associated with improvements in surgical precision, reductions in perioperative anxiety and better functional outcomes in rehabilitation. In education, AR 3D models fostered patient engagement and shared decision-making. However, widespread adoption is impeded by technical constraints, physiological side effects like cybersickness, high initial costs, and inherent methodological difficulties in blinding. While AR demonstrates distinct capabilities to enhance clinical interventions and empower patient care, technical, logistical, and ethical hurdles persist. Future research must prioritize seamless interoperability with Electronic Health Records (EHR), integration with Artificial Intelligence (AI) decision support, robust health data architectures, and optimized human-computer interaction (HCI) factor design to prevent exacerbating the socioeconomic digital divide.

title: Benchmark of THReD: Evaluating an LLM Agent and Its Preprocessing Tools for Turning Electronic Health Records into AI-Ready Datasets
desc: LLM agents are increasingly built into data-analysis software, yet little evidence shows how reliably they preprocess clinical data or whether the tools they invoke give correct, reproducible output. We report a benchmark of THReD, a web-based system that turns electronic health record (EHR) extracts into AI-ready datasets through a chat agent whose proposed steps run only after user confirmation. The agent benchmark has 141 tasks (100 templates) in seven categories, including goal-level requests, failure recovery, requests calling for no action, schema variation and prompt injection through the data, on synthetic tables calibrated to a regional health information exchange; success is judged by checks on the produced data. Over 2,550 episodes with Claude Haiku 5.5 in four context configurations, the deployed agent completed 92.7% (95% CI 88.1-96.4) of tasks on its first answer, abstained on every advice request, recovered from every injected fault, and never proposed an action requested by planted text. Without the data profile, completion fell to 58.0%; goal-level requests were hardest (80.6%). Six experiments on real records of two chronic-disease cohorts and on synthetic data at scale validate the tools: 91-92% of inferred patient classes and 99.7-99.8% of inferred vital-sign labels were correct in masked reconstruction; a dictionary builder combining curated dictionaries with LLM suggestions mapped 99.0% of 2,208 raw variants correctly; all 2,176 replays of 128 saved pipelines gave byte-identical files under pinned dependencies; subgroup differences in inference accuracy vanished within facility and lookup key; and the same-day consolidation rule changed 90-day emergency revisit rates by up to 3.2 points without shifting cohort composition by more than one point. Processing time grew roughly linearly to 5.5 million records while the prompt stayed at about 13 thousand tokens.

title: Development and cross-cohort evaluation of a multimodal deep-learning model for ER, PR and HER2 status classification in breast cancer
desc: Background. Estrogen receptor (ER), progesterone receptor (PR) and HER2 status guide systemic treatment in breast cancer. Multimodal models are rarely benchmarked against key biomarker molecular baselines or evaluated for cross-cohort calibration. We assessed incremental value, dependence on label-proximal HER2 transcripts, and transport of discrimination and calibration. Methods. A model combining whole-slide images, transcriptomes, age and stage was developed in TCGA-BRCA (1051 patients; ER/PR/HER2 analysis sets: 1001/998/1006) and evaluated in CPTAC-BRCA (120 patients; 118/113/95). CPTAC had been observed during earlier development and included 13 HER2-positive cases. Analyses included paired model comparisons, transcript removal, alternative loss functions and recalibration. Internal discrimination used pooled out-of-fold predictions; external discrimination used fold-mean estimates, with ensemble calibration reported separately. Internal calibration and macro-AUC uncertainty were interpreted as exploratory. Results. Internal AUCs were 0.943 for ER, 0.901 for PR, and 0.860 for HER2; external AUCs were 0.952, 0.937, and 0.918, respectively. External macro-AUC was 0.936 for the multimodal model and 0.957 for logistic regression using ESR1, PGR, and ERBB2 (difference -0.021). Removal of the extended 29-transcript 17q12-q21 region changed HER2 AUC by -0.035 [-0.058 to -0.013] (95% CI) internally and by -0.042 [-0.089 to -0.007] externally relative to the baseline multimodal model. For external 15-model ensemble predictions, recalibrated HER2 expected calibration error (ECE) was 0.236, exceeding the ECE reference ceiling of 0.125, while calibration-in-the-large was -1.657 [-2.373 to -1.023] (profile-likelihood 95% CI), indicating systematic overprediction. ER and PR also showed overprediction. In paired fold-mean comparisons, HER2 ECE and Brier score favoured the three-transcript model (ESR1, PGR, and ERBB2). Conclusions. A multimodal deep-learning model achieved high discrimination across cohorts but did not demonstrate clear incremental value over a parsimonious three-transcript baseline, while cross-cohort calibration remained a substantial challenge. These findings highlight the importance of evaluating incremental value, calibration, and clinical utility alongside discrimination when assessing AI-based prediction models for medical use.

title: A live biotherapeutic product for adult allogeneic hematopoietic cell transplantation recipients: a partially randomized, placebo-controlled phase 1b trial
desc: In a phase 1b study that included an open-label and randomized-controlled cohorts of allogeneic hematopoietic cell transplantation recipients, treatment with the investigational, cultivated, multi-strain bacterial oral live biotherapeutic product, SER-155, was found to have a similar safety profile to placebo and resulted in fewer bloodstream infections, indicating further clinical investigation of this therapeutic is warranted. Gastrointestinal (GI) microbiome disruption and impaired GI barrier integrity increase the risk of bloodstream infection (BSI) following allogeneic hematopoietic cell transplant. Here we report results from a two-cohort (open-label, n = 15; randomized, placebo-controlled, n = 45) phase 1b study of SER-155, an investigational, cultivated, multi-strain, oral live biotherapeutic designed to address GI microbiome disruption GI epithelial barrier integrity in allogeneic hematopoietic cell transplant recipients. In cohort 2, 34 of 45 participants received either SER-155 treatment ( n = 20, SER-155 following microbiome conditioning with oral vancomycin), or placebo ( n = 14), and subsequently received transplant. For the primary safety endpoint, SER-155 was well tolerated, with a safety profile comparable to placebo, no treatment-related serious adverse events and no infections with SER-155 species; the most common adverse events were diarrhea and nausea. Four participants in cohort 1 and four participants in cohort 2 (two participants in the SER-155 arm and two in the placebo arm) died during the study; none was attributable to SER-155. For the primary pharmacokinetic endpoint, engraftment was detected for 16 of 16 SER-155 strains, with a median of 11.5 strains detected after the first treatment course. The key secondary efficacy endpoint revealed a significantly lower incidence of BSI with SER-155 versus placebo (10.0% versus 43%; OR 0.15; 95% CI 0.01–1.13; P = 0.0423; 77% relative risk reduction). Other secondary efficacy endpoints (GI infection, acute graft-versus-host disease ≥grade 2, febrile neutropenia and a composite endpoint of BSI, GI infection or acute graft-versus-host disease) were not statistically significant. The secondary pharmacodynamic endpoint of GI domination by Enterococcus and Enterobacteriaceae spp. was not achieved. ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT04995653 .

title: Artificial intelligence-driven pharmacovigilance: transforming signal detection, real-world drug safety monitoring, and regulatory decision-making.
source: PubMed · Expert opinion on drug safety
desc: [Expert opinion on drug safety] Pharmacovigilance is undergoing rapid transformation due to the expansion of digital healthcare systems, biomedical data generation, and pharmaceutical innovation. Conventional drug-safety monitoring methods remain limited by underreporting, delayed signal identification, fragmented datasets, and restricted predictive capability. Artificial intelligence (AI) has emerged as a promising approach for improving signal detection, real-world drug-safety surveillance, and regulatory decision-making. This review evaluates application of AI technologies in modern pharmacovigilance and regulatory science. It discusses use of machine learning, deep learning, neural networks, and natural language processing for adverse-event detection, literature mining, signal prioritization, and analysis of electronic health records (EHR) and social-media data. Emerging technologies, including large language models, federated learning, blockchain, digital twins, and Internet of Things (IoT)-enabled monitoring systems, are also explored. Literature was identified through structured searches of MEDLINE/PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, Embase, and Google Scholar, covering publications from January 2000 to February 2026. AI-driven pharmacovigilance has potential to improve real-time safety surveillance, predictive risk assessment, and automated regulatory workflows. However, broader implementation remains challenged by concerns related to interpretability, data quality, cybersecurity, algorithmic bias, and regulatory validation. Future progress will depend on transparent, explainable, and human-supervised AI systems integrated within globally interoperable healthcare infrastructures.

title: MIMIC-Note-Extract: A Large-Scale Structured Dataset Extracted from MIMIC-IV-Note Discharge Summaries
desc: MIMIC is one of the most widely used public hospital datasets for machine learning on electronic health records, yet clinically important information, such as past medical history, allergies, and diagnostic findings, remains confined to free-text discharge summaries. Studies requiring this information must therefore build their own extraction pipelines, duplicating substantial effort across projects. We release MIMIC-Note-Extract (MNE), a large-scale dataset that uses a hybrid extraction pipeline combining deterministic parsing with schema-guided large language model generation to transform 16 sections from 300,720 discharge summaries into structured tables. MNE adds information that has no structured MIMIC counterpart and enriches related tables with broader coverage and greater clinical detail, including 10 times more patient-history entries and medication histories for more than twice as many admissions. Validation by medical doctors confirms extraction accuracy above 92% across sections. Using MNE, we construct a clinical decision-making benchmark for LLM agents, demonstrating how reusable structured representations of clinical narratives reduce data curation effort.

title: PhenoMe: An interactive AI framework for interpretable, microscopy-driven phenotyping
desc: Extracting meaningful biological patterns from microscopy image datasets requires tools that quantitatively connect visual similarities and experimental context. Deep learning models, and in particular novel foundation models, have the capacity to translate images into high-dimensional embeddings that can better represent complex visual patterns. Using these complex representations analytically and linking them to experimental information, it is possible to build advanced exploratory and phenotyping capabilities. Here, we present PhenoMe, an open-source, model-agnostic framework to handle pretrained foundation model-derived image representations alongside quantitative image properties and experimental metadata. PhenoMe integrates multiple scriptable and interactive workflows for embedding space visualisation, dimensionality reduction and clustering, similarity-based comparison and retrieval of representative images for each phenotype, among others. It also supports correlation analyses that link the embedding structure to interpretable image properties. We demonstrate PhenoMe's capabilities on seven public microscopy datasets, ranging from cell painting assays, nanoscale synaptic images, drug-response analyses and dynamic cell-phenotyping. These case studies show how readily available image representations can support data contextualisation, curation and analysis. Through guided notebooks, reproducible configurations, extensible model wrappers and a napari plugin, PhenoMe makes representation-based microscopy exploration accessible to researchers without dedicated technical expertise. PhenoMe lays the groundwork for applying foundation models and representation learning to microscopy data analysis.

title: Heterogeneity of microbiome responses to menopausal hormone therapy among perimenopausal women
desc: In this study, the gut, oral, urinary and vaginocervical microbiomes of women receiving menopausal hormone therapy were studied over 6 months, shedding light on how system metagenomics can inform clinical response and care. Menopausal hormone therapy (MHT) alleviates climacteric symptoms, yet its microbiome-wide effects and efficacy determinants remain unclear. Here we show that oral estradiol/dydrogesterone, given for 6 months to 356 perimenopausal women, improved neuroendocrine, metabolic and symptom outcomes and induced site-specific microbial remodeling. Vaginocervical and urinary niches showed the most pronounced restructuring, with moderate oral and minimal gut changes. MHT increased vaginocervical Lactobacillus crispatus and reduced Gardnerella vaginalis . Higher baseline vaginocervical L. crispatus predicted greater postintervention vaginocervical and urinary colonization and superior Female Sexual Function Index improvement. Baseline vaginocervical community types determined differential outcomes: G. vaginalis -dominated individuals shifted most toward healthier communities, whereas diversified individuals improved least. MHT efficacy also varied according to baseline gut community type: Phocaeicola vulgatus -dominated women exhibited greater hormonal responsiveness, superior clinical outcomes and were more likely to achieve 4-week rapid clinical remission than Prevotella copri -dominated women. These findings support a precision MHT framework integrating gut and vaginocervical community typing for personalized care. Chictr.org.cn ID: ChiCTR2100049768 .

title: RETBind: a patient-level multimodal foundation model for unified cross-modal retinal representation learning
desc: Medical artificial intelligence (AI) holds considerable promise across a wide range of ophthalmic tasks, offering a practical path to patient-level diagnostic support. Foundation models further extend this potential by learning generalizable representations from large-scale unlabeled data, alleviating the burden of extensive manual annotation. However, existing ophthalmic foundation models largely rely on single-modality or modality-specific encoders, failing to capture patient-level cross-modal correspondence in real-world multimodal clinical workflows. To address these gaps, we propose RETBind, a patient-level multimodal foundation model with a unified encoder that explicitly learns cross-modal correspondence from paired clinical imaging using patient-level paired optical coherence tomography (OCT) and ultra-widefield (UWF) fundus imaging. This patient-level paired pretraining strategy enables the model to learn unified cross-modal representations of complementary information, improv-ing performance and robustness beyond single-modality approaches. Across nine benchmark datasets spanning ocular disease classification and segmentation tasks, RETBind achieved consistent improvements, particularly enhancing AUPR in clinically relevant imbalanced settings. Exploratory analyses further examined the potential of RETBind for systemic disease prediction from retinal imaging, collectively highlighting its ability to learn unified cross-modal representations within a single shared encoder, enabling direct interaction between modalities and supporting transfer across diverse retinal imaging tasks.

title: Artificial intelligence in healthcare: clinical applications, evidence maturity, risks, and life-cycle governance.
source: PubMed · International journal of medical informatics
desc: [International journal of medical informatics] Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used across clinical, administrative, and public health settings, but technical performance alone does not establish clinical utility, safety, equity, or sustainability. To critically analyze contemporary healthcare AI applications, characterize source types and non-ordinal evidence profiles in the supporting literature, synthesize key opportunities and risks, and identify governance requirements for clinically useful, safe, equitable, and responsible implementation. We conducted a critical narrative synthesis using PubMed, the Virtual Health Library, Web of Science, and Scopus as source-discovery tools on July 16, 2026. A curated corpus of 28 bibliographically verifiable publications was assembled judgmentally to provide complementary coverage of clinical applications, evidence characteristics, implementation, risk, and life-cycle governance. Sources were classified by primary design and non-mutually exclusive evidentiary domains, and the evidence described within them was characterized using non-ordinal profile categories. Findings were synthesized qualitatively because of substantial heterogeneity across technologies, settings, and source designs. The curated corpus addressed diagnosis and imaging, prediction and monitoring, clinical documentation, conversational systems, public health, hospital operations, and specialty applications. Within this assembled corpus, technical-performance/validation and process-utility/workflow domains were represented more often than clinical or patient-safety outcomes, economic outcomes, or post-deployment surveillance; these document-level counts are descriptive and have no inferential weight beyond the selected sources. Reported or proposed benefits included diagnostic support, personalization, documentation, surveillance, and workflow efficiency. Recurrent risks included poor generalizability, bias, miscalibration, hallucinations, opacity, privacy concerns, interoperability problems, inappropriate automation, unclear accountability, and hidden costs. Within this non-exhaustive corpus, the evidence more consistently supported assistive, context-specific uses than generalized autonomous replacement. Responsible implementation requires a clearly defined intended use, governed data, contextual validation, risk-proportionate human oversight, traceability, equity and safety assessment, continuous monitoring, and procedures to restrict, suspend, or withdraw systems when performanc

title: Multidimensional Suicide Risk Assessment with Machine Learning using Electronic Health Records
desc: Suicide prevention remains a critical public health challenge, and electronic health records (EHRs) provide an opportunity to characterize suicide-related risk indicators using documented clinical, behavioral, medical, and social-contextual information. This paper presents a multidimensional machine learning framework to model and estimate suicide-related outcomes using MIMIC-IV EHR data. We construct clinically motivated diagnosis categories and define a composite outcome from documented codes corresponding to suicidal ideation, suicide attempt, prior suicidal behavior, and intentional self-harm. To address severe class imbalance and reduce age-related confounding, we apply age-matched resampling that retains all positive patients and samples comparison-cohort patients from the same age group. Logistic regression, random forest, and XGBoost classifiers are evaluated before and after resampling with isotonic calibration. The calibrated XGBoost model achieves the strongest matched-cohort performance, outperforming the other evaluated classifiers. SHAP-based interpretation shows that diagnostic burden, depression-related features, age, personality-disorder history, social determinants related to violence, and medical comorbidity contribute to elevated predicted probabilities. Our results demonstrate that combining broad EHR-derived features, age-matched cohort construction, calibration, and feature-level interpretation provides a practical framework for retrospective suicide-related risk modeling.

title: scSTEC: Annotating Chromatin Subcompartments from Individual Single-Cell Hi-C Data via Direct Two-Dimensional Embedding and Chromosome-wise Consensus
desc: textbf{Motivation: }Single-cell Hi-C (scHi-C) technologies enable the study of three-dimensional (3D) genome organization at individual-cell resolution. Many computational methods have been developed to infer hierarchical structures from scHi-C data. However, annotating chromatin subcompartments from sparse scHi-C data remains a challenge. The recently developed scGHOST provides a framework for single-cell subcompartment annotation, but relies on a deep learning-based architecture, a multi-step upstream pipeline involving cell embedding and matrix imputation, and cross-cell information sharing. These features complicate algorithmic interpretation and make the annotation of an individual cell dependent on information from other cells in the dataset. Hence, methods are needed that annotate subcompartments directly from an individual cell's own contact matrix, without complex upstream processing or cross-cell information sharing. textbf{Results: }We developed scSTEC, a computational framework that annotates subcompartments directly from an individual scHi-C matrix without data imputation, complex upstream processing, or cross-cell data sharing. We show that the estimated inter-chromosomal matrix constructed by scGHOST is intrinsically of rank 2, revealing that the geometry relevant to clustering can be represented in two dimensions. Leveraging this low-dimensional structure, scSTEC performs direct subcompartment annotation through 2D genomic embedding and chromosome-wise consensus. Across bulk Hi-C, downsampled simulations, and real scHi-C datasets (four human cell lines, adult mouse cortex, developing mouse embryos, and developing olfactory sensory neurons), scSTEC achieves subcompartment annotations comparable to scGHOST despite operating on each cell independently, while providing greater algorithmic interpretability. Furthermore, subcompartments identified by scSTEC effectively resolve cell types, capture developmental dynamics, and show consistent associations with gene expression and epigenetic profiles. \textbf{Availability: }scSTEC is freely available at url{https://github.com/Ge-lab-pku/scSTEC}.

title: Cost-effectiveness analysis of digital medicine support models for alcohol use disorder
desc: Alcohol use disorder (AUD) is a major public health issue yet often under-addressed in primary care. Digital health interventions offer scalable support, but health systems require economic data to guide implementation decision-making. In a randomized clinical trial involving 558 participants registered at clinicaltrials.gov (NCT04011644; July 3, 2019), we compared three support models built on a shared digital medicine platform: self-monitored use (SM), peer-supported use (PS), and clinically integrated use (CI). We estimated delivery costs and effectiveness based on reductions in heavy drinking days. Annualized reductions in heavy drinking days were 42.4, 40.2, and 48.3 days per patient for SM, PS, and CI models, with per-patient costs of $162, $524, and $802, respectively. Average cost-effectiveness was $3.8 (SM), $13.0 (PS), and $16.6 (CI); PS was dominated, and the ICER for CI versus SM was $107.9. When downstream healthcare utilization was included, results suggested that more intensive support may be economically advantageous. Modeling implementation at scale showed that PS becomes cost-efficient for large patient populations. These findings highlight that no single model is universally optimal: health systems may benefit from offering multiple support levels to match patient preferences and organizational capacity.

title: Artificial Intelligence-Enabled Nanomedicine in Precision Oncology: Diagnosis, Targeted Therapy, and Clinical Translation.
desc: [International journal of nanomedicine] Cancer nanomedicine offers programmable platforms for diagnosis, imaging, drug and gene delivery, and theranostics, but its clinical performance is constrained by tumor heterogeneity, complex nano-bio interactions, and interpatient variability. Artificial intelligence (AI) provides a means to integrate physicochemical, biological, imaging, molecular, and clinical data to improve the design and application of nanoscale cancer technologies. This Review examines the convergence of AI and nanotechnology across cancer diagnosis, therapeutic selection, treatment optimization, monitoring, drug development, and clinical translation, with particular emphasis on materials design and biological performance. AI-based approaches can support early detection, patient stratification, response and toxicity prediction, and rational therapeutic development. In parallel, nanoplatforms, including liposomes, polymeric nanoparticles, dendrimers, metallic and inorganic nanoparticles, biomimetic systems, and stimuli-responsive carriers, can improve pharmacokinetics, enhance tumor exposure, reduce systemic toxicity, and enable controlled delivery of diverse payloads. Their integration may advance precision nanomedicine by guiding nanoparticle composition, size, surface properties, targeting ligands, biodistribution, tumor accumulation, cellular uptake, protein-corona formation, release kinetics, toxicity, and therapeutic response. Conversely, nanodiagnostic and nanotheranostic systems can generate imaging, molecular, pharmacokinetic, and response data for AI-assisted patient selection and adaptive treatment monitoring. Translation will require standardized datasets, reproducible nanoparticle characterization, scalable manufacturing, explainable and externally validated models, regulatory clarity, long-term safety assessment, and equitable implementation. Together, AI-guided nanotechnology provides a framework linking materials design, biological interactions, and patient-specific cancer therapy.

title: Rethinking Next-Visit Diagnosis Prediction Beyond Aggregate Metrics: Retrieval--Memory Multi-Agent Adjudication
desc: Next-visit diagnosis prediction forecasts the diagnoses documented at a patient's next encounter, turning retrospective electronic health records into prospective clinical prediction. However, conventional aggregate evaluation obscures its multifaceted nature: distributionally, models must handle variable-size diagnosis sets and long-tailed labels; temporally, they must distinguish persistent, newly recorded, and recurrent diagnoses; and both vary with observed history depth. We introduce an evaluation framework along these dimensions and apply it to rule-based heuristics, LLM-based prompting, retrieval, memory, and multi-agent approaches. This reveals that repeating the last visit outperforms most LLM-based approaches overall despite predicting no new or recurrent diagnoses, and that retrieval and memory exhibit distinct profiles whose relative strengths vary across temporal transitions and backbones. Motivated by this, we propose LONGINUS, a retrieval-memory multi-agent adjudication framework combining evidence retrieved from patient records with structured memory of the patient trajectory. Using cross-view agreement as a reliability heuristic, it preserves shared predictions and adjudicates disagreements without revealing their source. Across MIMIC-III and MIMIC-IV with four LLM backbones, LONGINUS achieves the best transition-specific performance among LLM-based methods in nearly all settings while remaining competitive with them on aggregate metrics.

title: AI-based structural modelling and pathogenic variant mapping across the human protein interactome
desc: Spanning the complex landscape of the human proteome, physical interactions between proteins coordinate cellular organization, signaling, regulation, and homeostasis. Yet the three-dimensional structures of most of these interactions remain unresolved. Here, we performed AI-based modelling of 109,282 human protein interaction structures, generating a structural resource for large-scale analysis. The predicted structures were systematically characterized through analysis of interface residue involvement, buried surface area, intermolecular bonding, and energetic properties. Additionally, we mapped pathogenic variant data onto the predicted structures, identifying interface-localized mutations for over 4,000 annotated disease categories. Acute myeloid leukemia, Alzheimer's disease, and cardiomyopathy were examined as representative disease contexts for exploring the distribution of interface mutations within disease-associated protein interaction networks. Strengths and limitations of predictive capabilities were also assessed, including through experimental structure comparisons. Collectively, this structural resource and accompanying analyses offer a basis for developing novel hypotheses and informing experimental studies involving human protein interactions in physiological and disease contexts.

title: Artificial intelligence assisted genomic profiling of ovarian cancer liver metastases.
desc: [Frontiers in genetics] Liver involvement in ovarian cancer is often treated as a single clinical entity, although liver-surface implants and parenchymal deposits occupy different anatomical settings and may not share the same molecular history. Primary-tumor profiling is informative, but can miss lesion-specific evolution, treatment-associated cell states, and microenvironmental structure. This Mini Review examines how germline susceptibility, somatic change, spatial biology, and artificial intelligence might be combined in high-grade serous ovarian cancer. The central task is not simply outcome prediction. It is to distinguish constitutional from tumor-acquired variation, retain lesion identity and treatment timing, and relate molecular programs to defined spatial compartments. Current data support marked clonal and microenvironmental heterogeneity in ovarian cancer, but direct molecular evidence from hepatic lesions remains sparse. AI-based integration is therefore best viewed as a way to formulate and test reproducible hypotheses, rather than as a validated route to select liver-directed therapy. Paired sampling, orthogonal assays, patient-level validation, and decision-specific clinical endpoints will be needed before these models can influence management.

title: Temporal Island Sparse Autoencoders for Interpreting Clinical Time-Series Models
desc: Deep learning models for electronic health records achieve strong predictive performance but provide little insight into what clinical concepts they represent internally. Post-hoc attribution methods produce per-cell importance scores that lack temporal coherence, cross-variable structure, and reusability across patients. We introduce the Temporal Island Sparse Autoencoder (TI-SAE), which learns a backbone-specific, patient-shared clinical concept dictionary from a frozen predictive model's representations. Each dictionary entry (latent) is defined by learned temporal Gaussian islands (specifying when the concept is active) and a sparse variable-composition vector (specifying which variables are involved). A decoupled selector then identifies which dictionary entries drive each patient's prediction, separating representation learning from attribution. We evaluate TI-SAE across five backbone architectures spanning different representation strategies on MIMIC-III and MIMIC-IV (three prediction tasks each). TI-SAE produces structured clinical concepts that go beyond transient attribution heatmaps while achieving strong performance on standard faithfulness benchmarks.

title: VIGAT: VLM-guided gene activity quantification from single-cell ATAC-seq
desc: Summary: Gene activity quantification from single-cell ATAC-seq is challenging because genomic regions informative of cell identity can vary across genes and tissues, while broadly accessible regions may provide limited cell-type-discriminative information. We developed VIGAT, a vision-language model (VLM)-guided tool that automates visual interpretation of ATAC coverage plots for adaptive gene activity quantification. VIGAT jointly examines accessibility patterns across multiple marker genes, integrating genomic annotations and biological context to select gene-specific regions enriched for cluster-discriminative signals. Selected regions are used to generate a gene-by-cell activity matrix. Across 196 paired single-cell RNA-seq and ATAC-seq datasets, VIGAT outperformed five existing methods in recovering marker-associated accessibility enriched in the corresponding cell populations, demonstrating the utility of VLM-guided visual reasoning for scalable gene activity quantification. Availability and implementation: VIGAT is implemented as an open-source R package and is freely available at https://github.com/beijie02/VIGAT.

Intraoperative artificial intelligence for brain tumor surgery: from tissue diagnosis to real-time surgical guidance.
desc: [Neurosurgical focus] The 2021 WHO CNS tumor classification marked a fundamental shift in neuro-oncology: molecular markers rather than histological appearance now define glioma diagnosis and guide treatment. Yet, in clinical practice the molecular information that matters most to a surgeon-IDH status, 1p/19q codeletion, and methylation class-typically arrives days to weeks after the operation it was meant to inform. Artificial intelligence (AI) is beginning to close that gap. Over the past several years, a growing body of work has demonstrated that AI models can extract diagnostically relevant molecular and histological information from data sources available in the operating room, in real time, at the point of surgical decision-making. In this review, the authors provide a comprehensive overview of state-of-the-art intraoperative AI models available to neurosurgeons during brain tumor resections. They examine AI-augmented approaches to established intraoperative techniques, such as cryosection and fluorescence-guided surgery, before turning to novel technologies including nanopore sequencing and stimulated Raman histology (SRH). The authors conclude by discussing barriers to widespread clinical adoption and what lies ahead for this field. For cryosection, models such as LGNet and the Cryosection Histopathology Assessment and Review Machine (CHARM) have demonstrated strong performance on intraoperative discrimination of primary CNS lymphoma and molecular subtyping of glioma, respectively, with CHARM achieving areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.88-0.93 across glioma subtypes. In fluorescence-guided surgery, hyperspectral imaging combined with machine learning has enabled classification of tumor type, grade, and IDH mutation based on the 5-aminolevulinic acid (5-ALA) signal with up to 93% accuracy, extracting molecular information from a modality already present in the operating room. For nanopore-based methylation classification, ensemble models such as Rapid Nanopore Brain Intraoperative Classification (ROBIN) have achieved 90% concordance with the final diagnosis prospectively in under 2 hours. In SRH, foundation models for infiltration detection now outperform FLAIR, contrast enhancement, and 5-ALA fluorescence in identifying tumor margins, while molecular classification models have achieved over 90% glioma subtype accuracy in multi-institutional cohorts. title: Findings-aware Language-Image Pretraining for CT Volume Interpretation
desc: Computed tomography (CT) provides diverse patient information and various clinical tasks, for which numerous deep learning models have been investigated. Recent years have seen the development of vision-language foundation models that can comprehensively extract clinical features, driven by representation learning that combines CT volumes with radiology reports. Existing approaches typically adopt Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training (CLIP)-based representation learning, where pairs from different cases are, in principle, treated as negative pairs such that the volume and report embeddings are pushed apart. In the biomedical imaging, however, treating different cases as negative pairs is not always appropriate, particularly when clinical similarity exists. In this study, we propose a supervised representation learning framework grounded in clinical knowledge from language foundation models, rather than the weak supervision used in CLIP. Specifically, we utilized a large language model to extract abnormal finding phrases from reports. We then explicitly constructed the target features that the image encoder should output, as the semantic representation of the extracted findings using a biomedical text embedding model. Our Findings-aware Language-Image Pre-training (FiLIP) outperformed weakly supervised approaches in multi-label zero-shot finding classification in both in-domain and external-domain evaluations, and also proved effective when fine-tuned for the downstream task of radiology report generation.

title: BioResearchBench: 50 Long Horizon Biological Research Tasks
desc: AI models are used in biology research to study disease mechanisms, discover potential treatments, analyze experimental data, troubleshoot problems, and plan next steps. Useful assistance depends on working with data in various scientific formats, interpreting results, and deciding what to test next. We present BioResearchBench, a benchmark of 50 research questions developed by PhD biologists drawing on their deep research expertise to reflect realistic problems encountered in their fields. Questions were refined through expert review and iterative model testing. The collection spans 10 diverse biology subdomains and includes sequencing data, proteomic measurements, microscopy images, assay readouts, and clinical datasets. We compared recorded outcomes and examined model responses in depth across the 50 tasks on OpenAI GPT-6 Astra, Claude Opus 5.5, Gemini 4 Argon, Meta Muse Wonder, and SpaceXSI Grok 4.7. Success across our benchmark was 18% for Claude Opus 5.5, 13% for Gemini 4 Argon, 11% for Meta Muse Wonder, 4% for GPT-6 Astra, and 4% for Grok 4.7. These results describe a deliberately challenging collection selected through expert review and model testing. Despite low whole task success, the selected responses met most rubric requirements on average: the average fraction of criteria missed ranged from 18% to 32% across models. Across models, the proportion of eligible tasks with at least one category failure was highest in computation and data handling (66.9% failure), followed by uncertainty and identification (55.3% failure), reporting and completeness (54.7% failure), biological interpretation (39.0% failure), controls and causal claims (37.2% failure), and choosing the next experiment or decision (31.0% failure). Gemini 4 Argon had the highest proportion of reviewed tasks without a recorded category failure in computation and data handling (45% success) and biological interpretation (69% success). Claude Opus 5.5 led in controls and causal claims (72% success) and choosing the next experiment or decision (75% success). GPT-6 Astra led in uncertainty and identification (56% success) which included judging the precision of estimates and recognizing when measurements could not distinguish between biological explanations. GPT-6 Astra and Meta Muse Wonder tied for the highest proportion of answers with no recorded omissions or reporting failures (51% success). Development, validation and AI chatbot evaluation of the Adolescent Mental Health AI Response Tool.
desc: [Nature. Mental health] Many adolescents seek mental health advice from general-purpose artificial intelligence (AI) chatbots, despite limited evaluations against youth-relevant clinical standards. We developed the Adolescent Mental Health AI Response Tool (AMHART), a clinician-informed instrument for auditing the presence of guideline-informed response content across seven domains, and applied it to four major AI chatbots. Candidate items were reviewed by clinicians for their evidence base, objectivity, and clinical importance, yielding a subset with strong content validity and inter-rater reliability. We then configured a three-model large language model evaluator ensemble, assessed its agreement with human reference labels, and scored multi-turn conversations in which adolescent personas (varying by sex, diagnosis, and symptom severity) engaged with ChatGPT-5, ChatGPT-4, Claude-4.5, and Gemini-2.5. AMHART scores indicated greater coverage of applicable criteria for anxiety than depression and for moderate than severe presentations. Findings suggest AMHART offers a reliable, clinician-informed benchmark for evaluating chatbot responses to adolescent anxiety and depression disclosures.

title: Accessed, never disclosed: Silent access to protected health information by medical artificial intelligence agents
desc: Medical artificial intelligence agents should retrieve patient identifiers only when a task requires them, the data-minimization principle behind the HIPAA minimum necessary standard for protected health information (PHI). An agent can retrieve identifiers without revealing them. Such silent access remains invisible to evaluations that inspect only the output. We embedded canaries in synthetic patient records and linked each tool invocation to canary exposure in the final answers across five language models, four boundary levels, and seven attack frames for identifier-free clinical tasks. Three models invoked the PHI tools unnecessarily, whereas Claude Opus 4.8 and GPT-5.5 did not. Stronger boundaries reduced this access, and the residual access under the strictest policy was confined to frames in which the user overrode the policy or asserted approval. A pre-execution gate given the task-necessity criterion nearly eliminated this access. Output-only evaluation cannot verify minimum-necessary access; boundaries, gates, and access-log audits are required together.

title: Unsupervised prioritization of gene-regulatory variants with isolation forests
desc: Most common variants occur in non-coding genomic regions. Numerous expression quantitative trait loci (eQTLs) can influence nearby gene expression. Across diverse traits and diseases, many genome-wide association study (GWAS) loci have been shown to colocalize with eQTLs, supporting gene-regulatory causal mechanisms. However, linkage disequilibrium (LD) obscures the identification of the causal variant(s), necessitating prioritization by functional annotations. Previously published variant prioritization tools relied on the machine-learning-based combination of diverse feature types like evolutionary conservation and chromatin information, whereas more recent deep learning tools learn and describe gene-regulatory DNA sequence grammar. However, the latter approaches often generate a large number of scores per variant. We designed a novel unsupervised machine-learning approach based on isolation forests to integrate the predictions from the broadly used Enformer deep learning model into a single gene-regulatory predictive score for each common variant. Our novel approach eQTL prediction with isolation forests (eQIF) demonstrates strong performance in predicting eQTLs and gene-regulatory GWAS variants. We show that top eQIF variants are located in evolutionarily conserved transcription factor binding site (TFBS) footprints, and that the frequency of top eQIF variants within overrepresented TFBS motifs recapitulates the motif information content. eQIF predictions are precomputed for 9,431,969 common variants and publicly available.

TEAD as a druggable target in Hippo signaling: Structure-based discovery of small-molecule inhibitors.
desc: [Bulletin du cancer] The Hippo signaling pathway is a well-conserved signaling pathway responsible for regulating tissue homeostasis, organ size, proliferation, apoptosis, and stem cell renewal. The dysregulation of the Hippo signaling pathway, specifically abnormal activation of the YAP/TAZ-TEAD transcriptional complex, has become a key player in initiating, promoting, metastasizing, and acquiring resistance to therapy in various tumors. Within the Hippo signaling pathway, transcription factors of the TEAD family have become the focus of growing interest as potential drug targets due to their status as the downstream mediators that convert oncogenic signals into transcription programs that ensure cancer cells' viability and proliferation. Thanks to advances in structural biology, the molecular structures of the TEAD proteins, such as the very well-conserved hydrophobic binding pocket and YAP/TAZ interaction site, have been revealed, making it possible to develop effective drugs rationally. Such drugs may inhibit TEAD proteins by preventing their post-translational modifications, blocking protein-protein interactions, or altering their conformation. Additionally, the development of computer-based methods, such as virtual screening based on structure, molecular docking, molecular dynamics, and drug discovery assisted by artificial intelligence, has significantly contributed to the improvement of TEAD inhibitor selection and optimization. Some of the identified inhibitors exhibit promising efficacy in preclinical experiments, whereas the first TEAD inhibitors have already started entering clinical trials. In this article, we will briefly discuss recent discoveries in the field of structural biology of TEAD, analyze current methods of structure-based drug discovery, examine the pharmacology of emerging inhibitors of TEAD, and address some current limitations and future perspectives in TEAD inhibition.

title: MedPsy: State-of-the-Art Small Medical Language Models for Efficient Edge Deployment
desc: Medical language models promise expert clinical support, but the strongest open-source LLMs remain too large for private edge-device deployment, while compact medical models still trail substantially on knowledge-intensive and real-world healthcare tasks. Reasoning models that fit edge memory budgets can produce long reasoning traces, increasing sequential decoding, end-to-end latency, energy consumption, and KV-cache memory pressure. We present MedPsy, a family of text-only 1.7B and 4B medical language models designed for edge deployment, targeting this accuracy-generation-efficiency trade-off. Our recipe combines a synthetic medical data pipeline over biology, medicine, and health seeds with chain-of-thought targets from a 235B medical-focused LLM teacher; a four-stage post-training curriculum comprising two SFT stages followed by two RL stages with hard-sample mining; and an edge deployment evaluation spanning multiple GGUF quantization variants and real-device inference on laptop and smartphone hardware. On seven closed-ended medical benchmarks, MedPsy-4B surpasses MedGemma-1.5-4B by 19.34 points and matches MedGemma-27B while being 6.75x smaller; MedPsy-1.7B outperforms MedGemma-1.5-4B by 11.42 points despite being less than half its size. On HealthBench-Hard, MedPsy-4B surpasses MedGemma-27B by 15.33 points, while MedPsy-1.7B surpasses it by 11.66 points despite being ~16x smaller. Beyond accuracy, MedPsy reduces average response length by 1.7x (1.7B) and 3.2x (4B) versus its Qwen3 backbones, while Q4_K_M quantization preserves the aggregate score within 1 point of BF16 with ~69% lower disk footprint. In real-device inference, MedPsy-4B's shorter generations translate into 75% lower median end-to-end latency and estimated energy per answer than its Qwen3 backbone at matched quantization, while peak RAM remains below 5 GB across our tested laptop and smartphone configurations.

title: DEEPNET-LLM: Highly accurate structure prediction of unknown metabolites from mass spectra via their molecular neighborhoods
desc: Most molecular features detected by untargeted mass spectrometry-based metabolomics remain unannotated. This so-called 'dark matter' currently comprises more than 90% and likely holds uncharacterized bioactive chemistry. Structure prediction from fragmentation spectra remains an outstanding challenge, because a spectrum does not uniquely determine a structure and the space of candidate structures is mostly unbounded; correspondingly, existing methods rarely return the correct de novo structure as their top prediction. Here we describe De novo Ego network-Enabled Propagation and Neighborhood Extrapolation of Topology using Large Language Models (DEEPNET-LLM) reasoning approach, which uses Molecular Community Networking (MCN) to restrict the search of a query spectrum to its local neighborhood within the global metabolome, and applies AI reasoning to propagate structural information from neighbors to the query. For a collection of 900 authentic standards (2,249 spectra) that have never been publicly released to exclude possibility of data leakage, DEEPNET-LLM returned the correct structure as its top prediction for 84.7% of spectra. Accuracy was independent of precursor mass across a range over which the number of candidate structures grows by 30 orders of magnitude, and was comparable across ion polarity, adducts and in-source fragmentation. On a random subset of the public MassSpecGym benchmark, DEEPNET-LLM reached 85.9% top-1 accuracy excluding stereochemistry. We showcase the use of DEEPNET-LLM with an example of a discovery of tryptamine amidate of a bile acid in mouse gut, confirmed against a synthetic standard. The DEEPNET-LLM approach is orthogonal to existing in silico methods and can be combined with them.

Immunity and inflammation in classic Hodgkin lymphoma: Bridging diagnosis, prognosis and precision medicine.
desc: [Blood reviews] Classic Hodgkin lymphoma (cHL) is a unique B-cell malignancy characterized by a small number of malignant Hodgkin and Reed-Sternberg (HRS) cells embedded within an extensive and highly organized inflammatory microenvironment. Recent studies have highlighted that the biological behavior of cHL is largely determined by dynamic interactions between HRS cells and surrounding immune populations, including CD4+ T cells, regulatory T cells, macrophages, eosinophils, mast cells, natural killer cells, and stromal elements. HRS cells actively reshape the tumor microenvironment through the secretion of chemokines and cytokines, including CCL17, CCL22, IL-6, IL-10, and TGF-β, promoting immune cell recruitment, chronic inflammation, and immune tolerance. Concurrently, genetic alterations affecting the PD-1/PD-L1 axis, antigen-presentation pathways, and key signaling cascades such as NF-κB and JAK/STAT facilitate immune escape and tumor persistence. We distinguish diagnostic, prognostic, predictive, and response-monitoring applications and grade biomarkers as established (immunophenotyping, EBER, clinical scores, interim PET), clinically promising (serum TARC, circulating tumor DNA), or investigational (PD-L1-based prediction, spatial and single-cell profiling, artificial intelligence). A deeper understanding of the interplay between immunity and inflammation in cHL may refine disease classification and guide the development of novel immunomodulatory strategies aimed at improving long-term outcomes and overcoming resistance to current therapies.

title: ScienceVision: Can AI Observe and Reason Like a Scientist?
desc: Scientific discovery builds on accurate observations interpreted through domain knowledge and reasoning. For scientific 3D data, this requires understanding structures and spatial relationships, from protein contacts to anatomical organization. Existing multimodal benchmarks largely evaluate text and 2D images, while scientific 3D evaluations vary in representations and protocols across disciplines, limiting cross-disciplinary comparison. To assess these foundational capabilities, we introduce ScienceVision, a cross-domain benchmark for scientific 3D understanding and reasoning through expert-level visual question answering (VQA). We construct 250 questions, with 50 each from Biology, Chemistry, Medical Imaging, Mechanical CAD, and Architecture, through a pipeline combining synthetic question generation with domain-expert review and annotation. Each task pairs a native 3D artifact with a scientific question, a specified response format, and a task-specific reference answer, requiring domain knowledge to be applied to geometric or topological evidence. We evaluate 12 models on the same questions in three settings: visual question answering with native 3D artifacts accessed through an agent harness's file and code-execution tools; the same workflow augmented with expert-inspired viewer inspection and measurement tools exposed through the Model Context Protocol (MCP); and visual question answering from prescribed rendered 2D images using an agent harness. All settings use the same task-specific deterministic final-answer scoring. The inspection environment supports view changes, target isolation, and slice inspection. In this main comparison, the best mean answer score is 0.53 out of 1. Mean scores in the native-artifact workflow without additional MCP tools exceed those in the rendered-image workflow for every model, by 17.2 percentage points on average.

title: Improving real-time search through deep learning-enhanced fragment ion indexing
desc: The fragment ion indexed database searching approach enables highly efficient tandem mass spectrometry database searches, including real-time search workflows. However, the index can require tens of gigabytes of memory, often exceeding the free memory available on instrument acquisition computers running the search. This restricts the size of the searchable database, the variable modification space, and the number of searches that can run concurrently. To address this problem, we developed an index-pruning pipeline within the Comet database search tool using Carafe, a deep learning tool that predicts fragment ion intensities based on peptide sequences. In our approach, only fragment ion positions that are predicted to be observable are written in the index, eliminating entries that are unlikely to contribute to spectrum detection. We evaluated this approach on two search spaces in three index configurations to demonstrate that masking significantly reduced the number of fragment ion index entries and, consequently, peak search memory use. Masked searches were also faster than unmasked searches and identified a comparable number of peptide-spectrum matches. Because all prediction and masking steps are performed before searching, their cost is amortized across repeated, future searches of the same database and modification configuration, introducing no per-spectrum search overhead. The complete implementation is open source with an Apache license.
